result:
The first thing that comes is the wind. Not a breeze, not a metaphor, just wind moving through an empty house at 3:17 a.m. I’m sitting on the floor of what used to be my childhood bedroom, now stripped down to bare pine and nail holes. The walls remember everything even if the posters are gone. That’s the cruel part of memory: it doesn’t need furniture.

I keep thinking about how we apologize to rooms when we leave them. We say “thank you” out loud to the air like idiots, as if the drywall might write us a recommendation letter. Maybe it should. I’ve been kinder to this room than I’ve been to most people.

Outside, the streetlight is doing that lonely orange thing it does, painting the driveway the color of old photographs. My mother’s car is still parked at the same angle she left it in 2019. Nobody’s had the heart to move it. The tires are flat now. Time wins again.

I brought a bottle of cheap red that tastes like cough syrup and regret. It’s the same brand we drank the night my brother told us he was sick. We laughed too loud at everything because laughing felt like defiance. Cancer hates laughter, we decided. We were wrong, but the delusion kept us warm for six more months.

There’s a particular cruelty in how specific grief gets. Not just “I miss him,” but I miss the way he said the word “actually.” I miss how he couldn’t pronounce “aluminum” correctly. I miss the stupid way he’d leave one sock inside out in the laundry like a signature. These are the details that murder you slowly, the ones that don’t make it into eulogies because they sound too small. But they’re the ones that follow you into grocery stores when you see the wrong brand of cereal.

I’ve been reading old diaries. Not mine. His. Found them in the crawl space like contraband from a war I didn’t know we were both fighting. The handwriting gets worse as the pages go on, like his body was slowly deleting the instructions for being human. The last entry is just a list of things he wanted to eat one more time:

- Perfectly ripe mango
- Mom’s terrible meatloaf (the one with too much ketchup)
- Those sour gummies from the gas station
- Snow

He never got the snow. Died in July like it was some kind of sick joke from the universe. I keep the list in my wallet now. Sometimes I buy the sour gummies and leave them on his grave like an idiot. The raccoons probably think I’m trying to summon something.

The wind picks up again. The house creaks like it’s stretching after a long sleep. I should probably be afraid of being alone here but I’m not. This place knows me better than any person ever has. It watched me learn how to be ashamed of my body. It watched me discover music that felt like being understood for the first time. It watched me become the kind of man who writes at 3 a.m. because sleep is just practice for dying.

I think that’s what we’re all doing, really. Practicing. Rehearsing our exit interviews with the universe. Making sure we have the right words ready when the lights go down. But the truth is there are no right words. There’s just the wind moving through rooms we used to live in, and the stupid hope that someone, somewhere, is still saying our names like they mean something.

The red wine is gone. My hands are stained purple like I’ve been crushing grapes or hearts. Same difference.

I stand up too fast and the room spins in that beautiful way that reminds you you’re still temporary. The floorboards sing their old song under my feet. I walk to the window and press my forehead against the cold glass like I did when I was seven and the world felt too big to ever understand.

Outside, the flat-tired car sits under the orange light like a patient animal. Waiting for someone who isn’t coming back. The mangoes are out of season. The snow isn’t due for months.

But the wind keeps moving through the house like it’s looking for someone. Like it has something to tell us if we’d just stay quiet long enough to listen.

I stay quiet.

The house stays quiet back.

And for one small moment, between the grief and the cheap wine and the 3 a.m. silence, it feels like enough. Not good. Not healed. Just... enough.

The wind dies down.

I whisper “thank you” to the room before I leave.

I think it whispers back.
